$doc: The data contract: the introspected schema merged with the authored sidecars and the engine registry snapshot. Generated — do not edit; `npm run contract:check` fails on drift.

analysis_results.tier_name: derived — a pure function of tier 2
analysis_results.grain: One entity's metrics from one run. `metrics` is jsonb rather than a column per measure on purpose: the set of measures is the analysis's business and adding one must not be a migration — which is the same argument the open `analysis_kind` enum makes, applied to the output side.

governance.note: Read follows the parent run's project reachability. No write policy and no user-facing write path: rows arrive only through `analysis_complete_run`. APPEND-ONLY AS A PROPERTY OF THE SCHEMA — `analysis_results_are_immutable` refuses every UPDATE, because a result that can be rewritten makes its run's key a lie: the key says these inputs and this code produced this answer. DELETE is not refused, and that is deliberate rather than an omission: rows cascade from `analysis_runs` and thence from `projects`, and refusing DELETE would make deleting an analysed project fail. Deleting a project is retention, not mutation of a result.

policies.name: analysis_results_select
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.analysis_runs r WHERE r.id = analysis_results.run_id AND public.has_project_access(r.project_id))
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.analysis_runs r WHERE r.id = analysis_results.run_id AND public.has_project_access(r.project_id))

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning.

columns.name: run_id
columns.meaning: The run that computed this. Every result reaches its dataset, its parameters and its code version through here — which is what makes a stored metric reproducible (T4) instead of a number with no provenance.

columns.name: entity_type
columns.meaning: What kind of thing the metrics are about — `node`, `project`, and whatever a later `analysis_kind` declares. Shape-checked only, for the same reason `analysis_kind` is: the catalog belongs in the contract, not in a CHECK.

columns.name: entity_id
columns.meaning: The entity's own id within the project, as the analysis names it (a node `uid`, a project id). TEXT because the analyses disagree about what an entity is and forcing one type here would force a migration the first time a new kind lands.

columns.name: metrics
columns.meaning: What was computed for this entity. jsonb so a new measure is not a migration. IMMUTABLE — see the governance note; recomputing means a NEW run, which is the point of the key.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: Row insert time, maintained by the database.

analysis_runs.tier_name: derived — a pure function of tier 2
analysis_runs.grain: One execution of one analysis for one project, identified by the world it ran against (`input_hash`), the parameters it ran with (`params_hash`) and the code that ran (`code_version`). Two runs carrying the same five-part key ARE the same run by definition, which is what makes serving a stored answer sound rather than a bet on how recently a timestamp moved.

governance.note: Read follows project reachability (`has_project_access`), uuid-only since WP 3.0. `write: null` is a STATEMENT, not an omission: there is no user-facing write path and there must not be one. Every write goes through `analysis_get_or_start`, `analysis_complete_run` and `analysis_fail_run`, each of which takes the actor as a PARAMETER and routes it through `assert_writer_may_act` — so the audit trigger names a person rather than recording `actor_known: false` (G4). There is deliberately NO write policy on this table, which makes `no-tier-skip` (I2) a property of the schema here rather than of today's callers. The RPCs AUTHENTICATE and do not AUTHORIZE: `20260917000005` removed a role gate from the shared preamble after it was found to refuse an organization admin on a live path, and making `min_project_role` load-bearing is D66 and WP 6.2's.

policies.name: analysis_runs_select
policies.using: public.has_project_access(project_id)
policies.with_check: public.has_project_access(project_id)

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning — the IDENTITY of a run is the five-column natural key, not this.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this analysis ran for. Referenced by uuid and never by a displayable name (`uuid-identity`, G1); cascades on project delete, which is retention rather than mutation of a result.

columns.name: analysis_kind
columns.meaning: WHICH analysis ran. Open enum — the CHECK constrains the shape to a lowercase identifier and the catalog of values is the `analysis_kinds` block above, so a new kind costs a sidecar edit and not a migration.

columns.name: input_hash
columns.meaning: WP 4.1's `current_graph_hash(project_id)` at the moment the run was claimed: the world this answer is about. This is the anchor invariant `input-hash` (I5) is about — and I5 is NOT met by this table alone, because I5 is about the DERIVED ROW carrying it. WP 4.3 stamps the same value onto the tier-3 rows the analyzers already write.

columns.name: params_hash
columns.meaning: SHA-256 of `params` as canonical `jsonb` text. Over jsonb and never over the text a caller sent, because jsonb normalises key order and duplicate keys — so the same parameters written two ways are one cache key rather than two.

columns.name: code_version
columns.meaning: WHICH code produced the answer. Part of the key so that a changed analyzer does not serve its predecessor's numbers, and so two versions can coexist on one input hash and be compared (§11's fourth exit check).

columns.name: params
columns.meaning: The parameters as sent, beside the hash of them, so a run can be read without reversing a digest. Immutable: re-pointing a stored run at different parameters would re-attribute an answer to a question it never answered.

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: `running`, `succeeded` or `failed`. Only a `succeeded` run is ever served as a hit — a `running` row is a claim somebody else is still working on and holds no results, and handing it back would render an empty analysis as a complete one. `failed` sits OUTSIDE the unique index on purpose (see `natural_key_unique`): otherwise the first crash would own that cache key forever and the analysis could never be retried on that input.

columns.name: started_at
columns.meaning: When the key was claimed. Part of the run's frozen identity, not of its state.

columns.name: finished_at
columns.meaning: When the run reached `succeeded` or `failed`. Null while running.

columns.name: duration_ms
columns.meaning: Wall-clock milliseconds from claim to finish. Reporting only — nothing keys on it, and a staleness rule that compared it to anything would be the timestamp comparison D12 is about.
columns.note: Nothing reads it, deliberately. It is here so a slow analysis is VISIBLE rather than inferred from two timestamps, and the moment anything keys on it we are back to asking whether a clock moved instead of whether the data changed — which is exactly D12.

columns.name: row_counts
columns.meaning: What the run produced, by entity type. Reporting and the Trust Report's input (A3); WP 4.4 assembles it.

columns.name: warnings
columns.meaning: The run's own account of its blind spots, carried with the result rather than left in a log — transparency commitment T3, which says every report states the known limits of its own computation.

columns.name: actor_user_id
columns.meaning: WHO asked for this run. NOT NULL, so a run that cannot name its actor cannot exist — the same stance `assert_writer_may_act` takes for the RPC writers (`20260917000005`). Note what attribution means here: the application authenticates against `approved_users` and not Supabase Auth, so the id is CLIENT-ASSERTED (D28) — the database refuses a write into a project the user cannot reach, which is a real constraint, but it is not proof of identity.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: Row insert time, maintained by the database.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: Last lifecycle change. The IDENTITY columns are frozen by `analysis_runs_identity_is_immutable`; only status, finish and reporting columns move, which is the line between what a run IS and what it is DOING.

weighted.meaning: Weight edges by `relative_revenue` rather than treating the graph as unweighted.

topology_digest.meaning: `public.network_topology_hash(project)` — a digest of the six columns `get_network_nodes_for_prominence` and `get_network_edges_for_prominence` return. IT IS AN INPUT TRAVELLING IN A PARAMETER AND THAT IS DECLARED HERE RATHER THAN HIDDEN: `current_graph_hash` covers eleven tier-2 tables and NOT `network_nodes`/`network_edges`, so without this the key cannot tell two different graphs apart and a re-uploaded network is served the previous graph's centralities as a hit. It belongs in `hash_network`; moving it there is a `schema_version` bump and a bump is unsafe until D70 lands, so WP 4.4 moves it and deletes this entry.

config.meaning: The caller's `ProminenceConfig` — the four weights and the two caps. It is part of the key because two configs produce two different scores over one graph. `null` means the analyzer's `defaultConfig`, which the function fills in before the digest is taken, so a stored run always records the config it actually used rather than the word "default".

topology_digest.meaning: See `network_metrics.topology_digest` — the same digest, for the same reason.

plant_name.meaning: The plant filter the request carried, or null for every row of the project. It is part of the key because two plants of one project are two different analyses over two different row sets. NOTE that `plant_name` is NOT project-scoped, which is why the function derives the project from the rows it loaded and refuses a set spanning two.

critical_nodes.note: NO `topology_digest`, and the absence is a statement: this analyzer reads `supply_chain_data`, which is `combine-project`'s output over the eleven tier-2 tables `current_graph_hash` already covers. Its inputs ARE in the anchor. The `threshold` parameter this block used to declare DOES NOT EXIST — `predictCriticalNodes` takes no threshold and the entry was authored from the plan rather than from the code. Removed in WP 4.3 rather than carried: an undeclared default is `declared-fallback` (I6) broken, and a DECLARED parameter that no code reads is the same defect pointing the other way.

combine_etl.computed_by: combine-project (migrated in WP 4.3, as §11 names it)
combine_etl.note: REGISTERED BUT NEVER SKIPPED. `combine_etl`'s output is rows in `supply_chain_data`, not entries in `analysis_results`, so "already computed" means "those rows are still there" — which the store cannot see, and a row deleted by hand would make a hit skip an ETL the project needs. WP 4.3 records the run for its identity; WP 4.4 owns staleness and is the package that may turn a hit into a skip.

governance.note: READ THE POLICIES BEFORE TRUSTING THIS ROW. The table carries two policies and they contradict each other: "Users can check their own login credentials" is `FOR SELECT USING (true)`, and "No direct access - use RPCs" is `FOR ALL TO authenticated, anon USING (false)`. Postgres policies are PERMISSIVE unless declared RESTRICTIVE, and permissive policies are OR'd — so the deny-all does not deny anything, and the intended rule ("no direct access") is not the enforced one. Whether that is reachable depends on the table GRANTs Supabase applies outside `supabase/migrations/`, which no static replay can see and which PLAN.md §15 is the way to settle. Recorded as D28 and assigned to WP 2.4, which owns the RESTRICTIVE-policy decision for the whole schema; it is named here because a reader of this page must not take `rls_enabled: true` for "reads are restricted".

This sidecar describes the table as the migrations now define it.

audit_logs.grain: One recorded action, on one plane. `admin` is what a super admin did, `data` is a tier transition — a write to tier 2, 3 or 4 — and `access` is a governed decision such as an export being allowed or refused.

governance.note: Two SELECT policies, and they are PERMISSIVE on purpose. A super admin reads every plane; an admin of the SAME ORGANIZATION as the actor reads that org's `data` and `access` rows. They grant DISJOINT slices, so the OR that D28 makes unavoidable is the intended union here rather than an accidental escape hatch — which is worth stating, because the same shape on `approved_users` IS the defect. There is no write policy: rows arrive from SECURITY DEFINER functions and from statement-level triggers, never from a client, so RLS denying writes by default is the enforcement (WP 2.2's pattern). `audited: false` on the audit table is not a joke — nothing records reads of it, and a deletion would leave no trace. Tamper-evidence is a Phase 4 question (hash-chaining a log is the same machinery as `input-hash`), not a WP 2.3 one.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The row's identity. Returned by the emit functions so a caller can cite what it wrote.

columns.name: actor_user_id
columns.meaning: Who did it. NULLABLE, and the null carries meaning: a service-role write with no session context has no attributable actor.
columns.note: THE HONEST LIMIT OF THIS TABLE. `audit_tier_write()` reads `get_current_user_id()`, which resolves only when the caller set `app.current_user_id`. The ingest and ETL edge functions run as the service role and do not, so their rows say WHAT changed and WHEN and record `actor_known: false` in `after` rather than inventing a WHO. That is worth having and it is not attribution; closing it means those functions setting user context, which is their change to make (§16, WP 2.3).

columns.name: action
columns.meaning: What happened. Admin-plane rows use the existing dotted vocabulary (`org.update`, `api_key.revoke`); data-plane rows use the SQL operation (`insert`, `update`, `delete`); access-plane rows use `export.allowed` / `export.refused`. Three vocabularies in one column, which is a cost of one table and is recorded here rather than discovered by a reader.

columns.name: target_type
columns.meaning: What kind of thing was acted on — a table name on the data plane, an entity name on the others.

columns.name: target_id
columns.meaning: Which one, as text. NULL on data-plane rows: a statement-level trigger records a STATEMENT, and a statement that touched 5,000 rows has no single id.

columns.name: before
columns.meaning: The prior state, where the writer knows it. Admin RPCs capture it; data-plane trigger rows do NOT — a statement-level trigger has the transition tables but writing 5,000 prior rows into one jsonb would make the log unreadable and unbounded. Their row COUNT is in `after` instead.

columns.name: after
columns.meaning: The resulting state, or — on a data-plane row — the shape of the statement: `tier`, `rows_after`, `rows_before` and `actor_known`. On an access-plane row it carries the decision and what was asked for.

columns.name: ip
columns.meaning: Caller IP where the writer recorded one. Never set by the triggers, which run inside the database.

columns.name: user_agent
columns.meaning: Caller user agent where the writer recorded one. As with `ip`, absent on trigger-written rows.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When it happened. Server-stamped, and the column the plane index orders by.

columns.name: plane
columns.meaning: Which plane the action belongs to — `admin`, `data` or `access`, CHECK-constrained. Added by WP 2.3; every row that predates it is `admin` by construction, because the only writer was `log_admin_action()`, which refuses anyone who is not a super admin.

substitutions.when: a row is written without naming a plane
substitutions.visible_as: the column default, which is also what makes the `admin_audit_logs` compatibility view writable for callers that have not moved yet

audit_logs.note: Coverage on the data plane is by TRIGGER, not by instrumented RPCs, and the difference is the point. WP 2.3's gap check measured 22 live SQL functions writing tier 2/3/4 with none emitting an audit row, plus six more write paths in edge functions running as the service role. Editing the 22 would have been the obvious reading of "emit on every tier transition" and would have missed all six, and would have missed the twenty-third function somebody writes next month. A statement-level trigger on each of the twelve tier 2/3/4 tables catches every writer that exists and every writer added later.

bom_multi_level.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
bom_multi_level.grain: One child-to-parent line of a deep bill of materials: this material is consumed by this higher-level component, at this level of the tree. Collapsed to effective product-to-material arcs before the engine sees it. UNIQUE on `natural_key_intended` since WP 3.3 (`20260916000018`), and the index is NULLS NOT DISTINCT because a ROOT line has no parent — without that clause the constraint would hold every line except the roots (D5 closed).

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this customer belongs to. Scoping is what makes `customer_id` a key: the same company in two projects is two rows, and merging them would merge two customers' models.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.meaning: The customer's identifier as the source file spells it. Joins to `outbound_logistics.customer_id`, which is the only place the identifier is used today — and the join is by string, untrimmed, which is D8's shape. IT IS ALSO THE UPLOAD KEY since WP 6.2 (§4 D108): the same string the outbound file spells, so a customer row and its lanes meet on the value the user typed rather than on a normalisation neither file performed.

columns.name: segment
columns.meaning: The customer's service segment, the axis the customer-echelon allocation policies tier on (`P-C.x`, blueprint §4.2 and Appendix A). NOT a closed vocabulary yet — there is no CHECK, because the set a CHECK would name is the user's own segmentation and inventing it before anybody can write the table is how a column gets a constraint nobody can satisfy.

engine.consumed_by: P-C.2 customer_allocation — Customer.segment, the axis `sla_tiers` keys its fill floors by, and what the `fill_rate_segment_<segment>` KPIs are named after
engine.missing_default: "default" (Customer.segment's own default) — every customer in one segment, so no `sla_tiers` key can match and every declared floor resolves to 0.0

ingest.validate: optional; any string. Blank lands NOTHING and the column's own DEFAULT 'default' stands in — which is a value and not an absence, so the landing reports it as a substitution rather than leaving the cell silent (T2).

columns.note: DEFAULT 'default' is production's own default, adopted rather than chosen. It is a value, not an absence, and a later reader must not treat it as "unsegmented" without saying so at the point of display (§5 T2). DECLARED IN WP 6.2 (§4 D94), which is what closed the blank above rather than the trace alone. `p_c2_customer_allocation.data_requirements` named one field — `outbound_logistics.volume` — while reading this column and `priority_weight` on every run, so `consumed_by: null` here had nothing to contradict it. The requirement is declared now, at level `defaulted` because `Customer` carries a default, and the gate that fell out of it is the inverse of the one `contract:generate` already enforces: an IMPLEMENTED policy's declared data requirement may not be `consumed_by: null` in the sidecar. TRACED IN WP 6.2 (§4 D69). This is the column whose absence was silent in a second way: `P-C.2`'s `sla_tiers` guarantees a fill floor PER SEGMENT, and the mapper gave every customer the entity default `"default"`, so no tier could ever match and every floor was 0.0. The engine already warned (`unknown_sla_segment` in P-C.2's feasibility) — the warning named the symptom while nothing named the cause, because the segments it compared against were a constant.

columns.name: priority_weight
columns.meaning: Relative allocation priority when demand exceeds supply. Dimensionless and relative — only the RATIO between two customers means anything, so a row at 1.0 is not "one unit" of anything.

engine.consumed_by: P-C.2 customer_allocation — Customer.priority_weight, the fallback ordering under the `priority` rule wherever the `priority_weights` param does not name the customer
engine.missing_default: 1.0 (Customer.priority_weight's own default) — every customer equal, so the `priority` rule cannot order anything

ingest.validate: optional; >= 0. ZERO IS ALLOWED AND MEANS SOMETHING: only the ratio between two customers matters, so 0 is the lowest priority there is — served last, and only out of what is left. `exclusive_min` would reject a value the engine reads correctly. Blank lands nothing and the DEFAULT 1.0 stands in, which makes the `priority` rule inert for that customer.

columns.note: TRACED IN WP 6.2 (§4 D69), AND THE PREVIOUS NOTE'S REASON WAS FALSE. It read: "`scsim` has no customer-priority concept today … none of [the `P-C.x` policies] is implemented". `p_c2_customer_allocation` is `status: implemented` in the registry export and has always read `Customer.priority_weight`. What was true is the CONSEQUENCE — nothing reached it — but the cause was the mapper never loading this table, not an absent policy, and the stated reason sent the next reader to the blueprint instead of to `project_map.py`. The blank was still correct while it lasted: `from_project_data` built `Customer(id=c, name=c)` from the outbound arcs, so every customer arrived at 1.0 whatever this column held. The mapper now reads it. AND IT IS DECLARED SINCE WP 6.2 (§4 D94). The mapper reading a column is the hop; the registry DECLARING it is what every tool deriving "what the engine reads" was missing — this sidecar, `project_map`'s requirement list and WP 6.1's resolution-chain door 1 were all blind to a field the engine consumes on every run.

columns.name: sla_fill_floor_pct
columns.meaning: The minimum fill rate the customer is contracted to receive, as a percentage. NULLABLE, and the null means "no contracted floor" — not zero. A reader that coerces it to 0 turns "unconstrained" into "no service required", which is D17's error in the other direction.
columns.note: NOT TRACED, and the REASON is now different from `priority_weight`'s — the two were given the same one and only this column's survives (§4 D69, D94). `P-C.2 customer_allocation` IS implemented, and it does guarantee fill floors: `sla_tiers`, keyed BY SEGMENT. This column is per CUSTOMER, and `Customer` has no field for it at all, so there is nothing to carry it into. Mapping per-customer floors onto a per-segment param needs a rule for what happens when two customers in one segment disagree, and inventing that rule is not a reader change. Declared gap, not a silent one.

customers.note: ADOPTED IN PHASE 3 / WP 3.0 (D43). This table existed in the production database with six rows and no creating migration, and it was invisible to the `no-orphan-table` gate for a reason worth keeping: R4 catches tables the CODE READS that no migration creates, and nothing has ever read this one. §15's schema probe — which keys on "production has it" rather than "the code reads it" — is what found it, and that probe now fails the verification run rather than reporting. TWO OF ITS COLUMNS ARE READ SINCE WP 6.2 (§4 D69): `segment` and `priority_weight` reach `P-C.2 customer_allocation`, because the mapper now loads this table instead of synthesizing `Customer(id=c, name=c)` from the outbound arcs. The sentence that stood here — "NOTHING READS IT YET, and the sidecar says so in every `consumed_by: null`" — was true of the outcome and wrong about the cause, and it gave that wrong cause twice more in the column notes below. It is not dead: its columns are the inputs of the customer-echelon policies (`P-C.x`), which is why it was adopted rather than dropped the way `product_code_map` was in the same migration. What it still lacks is a WRITER and a CSV template, and that gap is now BINDING rather than tidy: two of its columns reach the engine and no surface in this product writes them, so the values deciding who is served when supply is short can only arrive by hand in the database (§4 D94).

columns.note: `schema_version: 2` since WP 4.1 (`20260917000002`), and the shape changed with it: the tables now sit under two keys, `inputs` (what a SIMULATION reads) and `network` (what the multi-tier ANALYSES read), where v1 held them at the top level. A row written before that migration still holds the v1 shape and always will — nothing rewrites a frozen version — so any reader of this column handles both. `verifiableExports.ts` does. The rule for WHAT is in it changed too, and that is the point: v1 mirrored `datamap.py` by hand and missed three things as the engine moved on (D11, D67). v2 hashes every VALUE column of every tier-2 input table — everything but the surrogate `id`, `project_id`, the audit timestamps, the ingestion provenance and the cosmetic `name` — and `graphHashCoverage.test.ts` fails when a tier-2 value column is missing from it.

columns.note: D11 and D67 CLOSED by WP 4.1: the snapshot now covers `bom_multi_level` (which `datamap.py` PREFERS over the single-level table), `lead_time_unit`, `demand_min`/`demand_max` and `customers`, and every row ordering is the table's UNIQUE natural key rather than a hand-picked prefix, so the same data cannot hash two ways (D68). Equal hashes now prove equal inputs for every tier-2 table the contract describes; what they still do not cover is the four DERIVED network tables, which are WP 4.2's and deliberately out — a derived artifact inside the identity of its own inputs is the confusion I5 exists to prevent. COMPOSITE since WP 4.1: SHA-256 over `{schema_version, hash_inputs, hash_network}`, so it decomposes into the two columns beside it and `supabase/rehearsal/110` fails if it stops doing so. The name and the place in `simulation_runs` are unchanged on purpose (§11) — a rename is a migration across every reader.

WP 5.3 folded the deep-tier topology in to close §4 D75 — a re-uploaded network was being served the previous graph's centralities as a cache hit, because the anchor could not see the tables the two centrality analyzers read. The sidecar was not updated with the migration, and the manual renders this sentence, so the drift would have been published. delegation_grants.grain: One temporary, subtractive grant of project access from one person to another. `subtractive-delegation` (§2.1 G3) made real: a grant may never exceed what the grantor holds, and it always ends.

governance.note: `write: null` again literal. SELECT is limited to the grantor, the grantee and super admins; there is NO write policy, so RLS denies writes and `grant_project_delegation()` / `revoke_project_delegation()` are the only way in. That is forced rather than chosen: subtraction has to be CHECKED against the grantor's own level, and a PERMISSIVE policy cannot subtract (D28) — it can only add another OR'd way to say yes. `audited: false` is the uncomfortable one: a privilege grant that writes no audit row is exactly what `audit-actor` (§2.1 G4) exists to prevent, and WP 2.3 owns it. Recorded here rather than left to be noticed.

columns.name: updated_at

columns.name: lead_time_unit

ingest_files.grain: One file as received, in one run: the manifest for bytes held in storage — where they are, how many there were, and the SHA-256 of exactly the sequence received. Write-once: the row records an event that has already happened and cannot be edited into a different one.

governance.note: RLS reaches the project through the run, the same predicate the staging tables use. The grant is narrower than theirs on purpose — `authenticated` holds SELECT and INSERT and nothing else — because tier 0 is write-once and a grant that permits UPDATE would be a promise the trigger then breaks. columns.meaning: Surrogate key for one landed file.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The run this file was landed for. NOT NULL: a file with no run is a byte-stream nobody asked for, and making the run the owner is what keeps a landing attached to a project, a source kind and an approval.
columns.note: ON DELETE CASCADE, and the direction matters: deleting a project deletes its runs and therefore its file manifests. Tier 0 is immutable, not immortal — a RESTRICT here would have made a project undeletable, which is a defect dressed as rigour.

columns.name: source_kind
columns.meaning: csv, orbit-mrp or api — what kind of source produced these bytes. The same closed vocabulary as the run's.
columns.note: No default here either, and unlike the other two tables this column never needed a backfill: the table is new and has no rows to be wrong about.

columns.name: original_filename
columns.meaning: The file's name as the user's machine gave it, verbatim. For display and for the person's own recognition — never a key, and never parsed for meaning: two projects upload `inbound.csv` on the same afternoon (G1's rule, applied to filenames).

columns.name: storage_bucket
columns.meaning: The storage bucket the bytes live in. Recorded rather than assumed, so that moving a bucket is a data change and not a code change.

columns.name: storage_path
columns.meaning: Where the bytes are inside the bucket. Generated by the writer, never supplied by the user, and UNIQUE with the bucket because it addresses exactly one stored object.

columns.name: content_type
columns.meaning: The MIME type as reported at upload. NULLABLE and not trusted: browsers report `application/vnd.ms-excel` for CSVs often enough that a parser keying on it would reject real files. WP 3.2's parser decides from the bytes.

columns.name: byte_size
columns.meaning: How many bytes were received. The cheapest possible check that a file is the file somebody meant to send, and the number a quota will eventually be about.

columns.name: content_sha256
columns.meaning: SHA-256 of the bytes AS RECEIVED, lowercase hex, computed before any parse. The anchor: with it, 'the file you uploaded on Tuesday' is a checkable claim rather than a memory.
columns.note: CHECK-constrained on SHAPE (`^[0-9a-f]{64}$`) rather than on content, because a truncated or upper-cased hash compares unequal to itself and would break every lineage claim built on it — quietly, and much later. columns.name: uploaded_by
columns.meaning: The person who uploaded the file, in `approved_users`. NULL when the landing had no human — an API push or a scheduled pull — which is stated rather than filled with a service account.

columns.name: received_at
columns.meaning: When the bytes were received. Server-stamped, never the client's clock.

ingest_files.note: TIER 0, CREATED IN PHASE 3 / WP 3.1, AND NOTHING WRITES IT YET. PLAN.md §2 lists six tiers and this repository had five: there has never been a record of what a user actually uploaded. `UploadWizard` parses the file in the browser and throws it away, which is why every parse defect — D6's quoted comma, D7's blank numerics, D8's untrimmed identifiers, D46's integer `time_unit` — is unreproducible after the fact. You cannot re-read a file that was never kept. WP 3.2 is the writer: upload lands the bytes here, opens a run, and parses SERVER-SIDE. Landing the table one package ahead means that package does not have to invent a schema and a parser in the same session. WRITE-ONCE IS ENFORCED, NOT ASSERTED. `ingest_files_write_once()` refuses every UPDATE, and `supabase/rehearsal/060` proves it against a real database — both halves, because the rule is 'immutable' and not 'undeletable'. §2's tier laws have been sentences in a plan for three phases; a sentence nothing enforces drifts within two months, which is the lesson of the two orphan tables.

ingest_runs.grain: One ingestion attempt, from any source — a connector sync, a CSV upload or an API push — with the counts and the mapping report it produced. The unit a person reviews and approves: staged rows belong to a run, and promotion is a decision about a run rather than about a row.

governance.note: RLS keys on the run's own `project_id` — `has_project_access(project_id)` — which is WP 3.1's change. The original policy reached the project through `project_erp_links`, and a run with no link (`source_kind` csv or api) could not be reached that way at all: it would have been ungoverned rather than merely unsupported. `audited: true` SINCE WP 3.2, by the RPC route: `ingest_land_file` writes one `plane='data'` row naming the uploader and carrying this run's id when the run is OPENED, and `ingest_apply_run` sets `app.current_user_id` LOCAL to its own transaction before the tier-2 INSERT, so the statement-level `audit_tier_write` trigger names the promoter too. That is the half D36 said was expensive: it is cheap here because both functions take their actor as a parameter and neither depends on a GUC surviving PostgREST pooling. WHAT IS STILL NOT AUDITED: the CONNECTOR's runs. `erp-sync-orbit-mrp` writes this table as the service role with no actor to name, which is D36 proper and is WP 3.3's, unchanged by this package. `min_project_role: editor` states the intent — a viewer has no business opening an ingestion run — and nothing enforces the role yet; the policy is the modeler-or-admin predicate the connector shipped with.

columns.meaning: Surrogate key. Not the grain: a run is identified by what it did, and nothing joins to this except the staging rows and the landed files.

columns.name: link_id
columns.meaning: The ERP link this run used, or NULL for a source that has none. NULL means 'this source needs no link', never 'the link was lost' — a CSV upload and an API push have no credential to point at.
columns.note: Was NOT NULL until WP 3.1. Nullable is the widening: with it, a run belongs to a project rather than to a connector.

columns.name: triggered_by
columns.meaning: manual or scheduled. A manual run was asked for by a person; a scheduled one was started by the cron sweep against the link's `sync_schedule_cron`.
columns.note: Not an engine input. It is the field that decides whether `triggered_by_user_id` is allowed to be NULL — a scheduled run has no person, and saying so is `audit-actor` (G4) being honest rather than inventing an actor.

columns.name: triggered_by_user_id
columns.meaning: The person who asked for a manual run, in `auth.users`. NULL for a scheduled run, where there is no person — stated rather than back-filled to a service account, because 'nobody asked, the schedule did' is the true answer (G4).

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: running, staged, applied, failed or skipped. `staged` is the state that matters: rows are in tier 1 and a human has not approved them. Nothing reaches tier 2 before `applied`.
columns.note: Not read by the engine and never will be: tier 1 is invisible below it (I2). The readers are the review UI and the connector's own auto-apply gate, which refuses to promote a run with any `fields_failed`.

columns.name: rows_fetched
columns.meaning: Row counts pulled from the source, per entity — {"products": 1007, "bom_versions": 25}. What the source OFFERED, which is not what was staged and not what was promoted.

columns.name: rows_new
columns.meaning: Staged rows the diff classified as new: no live row carries this source identifier yet. For a file run this is `ingest_diff_run`'s count of rows whose natural key is absent from the tier-2 table, and it excludes the rows a later line of the same file superseded.
columns.note: WP 3.3 SET THIS TO INSERTS PLUS UPDATES. `ingest_apply_run` wrote `rows_new = v_total`, the total number of rows the upsert touched, and never wrote `rows_changed` or `rows_unchanged` at all — so the column named for one half of the split held the whole of it and the other two held zeroes that were not measurements. PLAN.md §4 D63; closed in WP 3.4 by computing the diff BEFORE the upsert and persisting what it found.

columns.name: rows_changed
columns.meaning: Staged rows whose live counterpart exists and differs.

columns.name: rows_unchanged
columns.meaning: Staged rows identical to their live counterpart. Counted rather than dropped: 'nothing changed' is a result, and a report that omits it cannot be distinguished from one that failed.

columns.name: rows_removed
columns.meaning: Rows present in the live table under this source and absent from the pull — `diff_state = removed_upstream`. Never promoted by the connector: a source dropping a row is not authority to delete the project's row. ALWAYS 0 FOR A FILE RUN, and that zero is a statement rather than a measurement: a connector pull speaks for the whole source, a CSV speaks only for the rows it contains, so an upload can never mark anything removed. The review screen says so in those words rather than rendering the zero (§5 T1).
columns.note: WP 3.3's `ingest_apply_run` wrote the count of rows HELD BACK by an error finding into this column — two unrelated facts in one place, and the one that was there was not the one the column is documented to hold. PLAN.md §4 D64. WP 3.4 gave the held-back count its own column, `rows_held`.

columns.name: mapping_warnings
columns.meaning: The per-field mapping report: [{level, entity, field, reason}], the same shape as `simulation_runs.mapping_warnings` and scsim's MappingWarning, so MappingWarningsCard renders it unmodified.

columns.name: fields_mapped
columns.meaning: Source fields that landed in a staged column with a value.

columns.name: fields_defaulted
columns.meaning: Source fields the source did not provide, left null for the project's defaults to fill at promotion. This is the count that drives the amber badge — a defaulted field is a substitution and §5 T2 says it is visible at the point of display.

columns.name: fields_failed
columns.meaning: Source fields that could not be mapped at all. A run with any failure never auto-applies, whatever the link's threshold says.

columns.name: diff_summary
columns.meaning: The rendered diff the review UI reads, kept until the run is applied or rejected. WP 3.4 builds that screen; the column is the connector's own and predates it.

columns.name: applied_at
columns.meaning: When the staged rows were promoted to tier 2. NULL for every run that has not been approved — which is most of them, by design.

columns.name: applied_by_user_id
columns.meaning: Who approved the promotion, in `auth.users`. NULL when the link's auto-apply threshold promoted it, and that NULL is the one D36 is about: an automatic promotion has no actor and says so rather than borrowing one.

columns.name: error_detail
columns.meaning: Why a failed run failed, in the source's own words. Kept verbatim: a paraphrased error is a second source for a fact that already had one.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the run opened. Server-stamped.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this run ingests into. Added in WP 3.1 and NOT NULL: it is what the RLS policy reads, so a run is governed by the project it writes to rather than by the credential it happened to use.
columns.note: Backfilled from `project_erp_links.project_id` for every row that existed. The backfill was total by construction — `link_id` was NOT NULL with a foreign key — which is why the migration sets NOT NULL without the guard `customers` needed.

columns.name: source_kind
columns.meaning: Where this run's rows came from: csv, orbit-mrp or api. CHECK-constrained, so a fourth source cannot appear without a migration that decides what it is.
columns.note: NO DEFAULT, deliberately. The column is backfilled to 'orbit-mrp' for the runs that existed and the default is then dropped, so the next writer must state its source. A default here would record a CSV upload as a connector sync and nobody would be told, which is the §5 T1 failure — a value with no provenance — inside the table that exists to record provenance.

columns.name: rows_held
columns.meaning: Staged rows carrying an `error` finding. They are never promoted and they stay in tier 1 with their reason attached, which is what makes a partial upload reviewable instead of a failure.

columns.name: rows_superseded
columns.meaning: Staged rows that a LATER line of the same file repeats on the natural key. The promotion collapses them (`DISTINCT ON`, so one statement cannot affect one row twice) and each one carries a `superseded_by_later_line` finding naming the line that beat it — the one case where the uploader's own file disagreed with itself.
columns.note: Counted separately from the three diff states, not inside them, so the five numbers partition the run exactly: new + changed + unchanged + superseded + held = rows staged. A review screen whose categories do not add up to the file is a screen that has lost rows.

ingest_runs.note: RENAMED FROM `erp_sync_runs` IN PHASE 3 / WP 3.1. The connector migration named it for the only source that existed and said in its own COMMENT ON TABLE that the name would be generalized in Phase 3; invariant `ingestion-contract` (I7) is why it had to be. A table whose name asserts one vendor cannot hold a second source's rows without lying about what it is. WHAT IS NOT HERE YET. Nothing writes a `csv` or `api` run: WP 3.2 builds the `ingest-file` edge function that does. The columns those runs need are here and described, which is the point of landing the schema one package ahead of its writer — WP 3.2 should not have to invent a schema and a parser in the same session. `supabase/rehearsal/050` and `060` assert what this table does: a connector run still stages, diffs and promotes identically, and a link-less run is legal and governed.

columns.note: Renamed from `synced_at` in WP 3.1: a CSV upload is not a sync, and the column had to mean the same thing for every source kind or it would have needed a second one.

columns.name: source_kind
columns.meaning: csv, orbit-mrp or api — where this row came from. CHECK-constrained, and it matches its run's value for every row any current writer produces.
columns.note: NO DEFAULT after the backfill: a writer states its source. Duplicated from the run deliberately — a staged row is read in bulk and joining to the run to learn what it is would make the common read the expensive one. If the two ever disagree the run wins.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key for one staged row.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The run these rows were staged in. NOT NULL, ON DELETE CASCADE: the run is the owner and the only route to a project, exactly as for `ingest_files` and the three connector staging tables.

columns.name: source_kind
columns.meaning: csv, orbit-mrp or api — the same closed vocabulary as the run's and the file's, CHECK-constrained with no DEFAULT.
columns.note: NOT AN ENGINE INPUT and never will be: tier 1 is invisible below it (I2). It is provenance, read by the review screen and by anyone asking where a tier-2 row came from.

columns.name: fact_class
columns.meaning: master or transactional — what KIND of fact one row is. Structure (a BOM) is master; a quantity over a period (a lane) is transactional. The value comes from the target table's own `ingest_dataset.fact_class`, so the contract decides it rather than the uploader.
columns.note: NOT AN ENGINE INPUT, for the same reason `source_kind` is not. It exists so that a later package can treat master data and transactional data differently at promotion without re-deriving which is which from the target table's name.

columns.name: target_table
columns.meaning: The tier-2 table these rows are destined for, by name. Not a foreign key — there is no table of tables — so `ingest_target_is_promotable()` is the closed set, and the landing refuses anything outside it before a row is written.

columns.name: source_row_number
columns.meaning: The physical line in the file, 1-based, counting the header as line 1 — so the first data row is 2, and the number matches what a spreadsheet shows the person who made the file. CHECK > 1 for that reason: line 1 is the header and can never be a staged row.
columns.note: This is the anchor WP 3.4's review screen clicks through to and WP 3.3's tier-2 `source_row_id` points at. It is also why a rejected row is KEPT rather than dropped: "row 42 is why" needs row 42 to exist somewhere.

columns.name: raw
columns.meaning: The cells exactly as the file gave them, keyed by the header the file carried — untrimmed, untyped, verbatim, including columns the contract does not know. The left-hand side of every parse claim.
columns.note: Keeping it is what makes D8 and D46 diagnosable rather than arguable: `" MAT-1 "` and `"MAT-1"` resolve to one id in `parsed` and remain two different strings here, and a `time_unit` of `21` is visible as the token it was rather than as the weekly it used to become.

columns.name: parsed
columns.meaning: What validation made of the cells, keyed by TIER-2 COLUMN NAME rather than by CSV header — the two differ, and the mapping is the contract's `ingest.csv_header`.
columns.note: A field that failed validation is ABSENT here rather than present as null. The distinction is the whole of D7: absent says "no value was established", null says "the file said empty", and a validator that spells them the same way puts 376 null volumes into tier 2 without telling anyone.

columns.name: findings
columns.meaning: [{level, field, code, message}] — the same four-key shape as `ingest_runs.mapping_warnings` and scsim's MappingWarning, so WP 3.4 renders it with `MappingWarningsCard` unmodified.
columns.note: A row carrying any `error` finding is never promoted — that is what "rejected with a row-level finding" means, and it is enforced in `ingest_apply_run`'s WHERE clause rather than hoped for. `warn` and `info` rows ARE promoted and shown, which is §5 T2: a substitution is visible at the point of display, not withheld by rejecting the row it is about.

columns.name: diff_state
columns.meaning: What this row is relative to the CURRENT tier-2 table — new, changed or unchanged — computed by `ingest_diff_run` at landing, again when the review screen is opened and again inside `ingest_apply_run` immediately before the upsert. NULL means the diff has not been computed for this row: a row held back by an `error` finding may have failed on a key field and so has nothing to compare. The CHECK also admits `removed_upstream`, which is the same vocabulary the three connector staging tables use so that one review component serves both sources; nothing writing THIS table ever sets it.

ingest.validate: one of new, changed, unchanged, removed_upstream

columns.note: NULL IS "NOT COMPUTED", AND IT REPLACED A DEFAULT THAT WAS AN ANSWER. Until WP 3.4 this column was `NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new'` and no code path wrote it — `20260916000019` does not mention it once — so every staged row claimed `new`, including the rows the upsert UPDATED, and a review screen reading it would have rendered "340 new" for 340 unchanged rows with a number and no hedge. PLAN.md §4 D62. A file run never writes `removed_upstream`: a connector PULL is a statement about the whole source and a FILE is not — nothing about one upload says it is the complete set of a project's rows, so an absent row means the file does not mention it, and `ingest_runs.rows_removed` is 0 for every file run.

columns.name: staged_at
columns.meaning: When the row was staged. Server-stamped, never the client's clock.

ingest_staged_rows.note: TIER 1, CREATED IN PHASE 3 / WP 3.2 — the fourth staging table and the last one of its kind. The three `ingest_staged_*` tables WP 3.1 renamed are TYPED against one source's entities (`external_id`, `sku`, `cycle_time_seconds`) because the connector knows what an orbit-mrp product is. A CSV of `inbound_logistics` is none of those things, and widening those three to hold it would have made each of them a table about two unrelated grains. So this one is generic where they are specific, and the generality is `ingestion-contract` (I7) working as intended: a new source lands here and never touches a tier-2 schema. WHAT IT CLOSES: the CSV path is the first in this repository for which `no-tier-skip` (I2) is true rather than aspirational. Before WP 3.2 a browser parsed the file and inserted straight into `inbound_logistics`.

materials.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
materials.grain: One material in one project: the economics the simulation reads for it. The precision path — the CSV lanes carry prices too, and where this row is silent the engine derives the value from them rather than treating it as missing.

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all thirteen sidecars change together. SEPARATELY — AND THIS REPLACES WHAT WP 1.2 WROTE HERE, WHICH WAS WRONG: this sidecar used to assert `rls_enabled: false` and say "no migration ever runs ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on them". One does. `20260614000001_item_master.sql:57-66` enables RLS and creates two policies (`%s_auth_all`, `%s_anon_read`) on each of the three masters — but through `EXECUTE format(...)` inside a `FOREACH` over an array of table names, which a static replay of the migrations cannot evaluate. The introspector recorded the absence as `enabled: false`, WP 1.2 read that as fact, and the contract was one generated page away from telling a user their item masters were unprotected. WP 1.4 fixed the mechanism, not the guess: the introspector now records dynamic DDL (`dynamic_ddl`) and marks the tables it touches `rls.determinate: false`, the validator refuses to let a sidecar assert an RLS state the migrations do not settle, and the generated page says the state is indeterminate and names the migration. The ONLY way to know is to read the live database — PLAN.md §15, still unrun. WP 2.4's security review owns it.

constraints.name: materials_source_row_fk
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (source_row_id) REFERENCES public.ingest_staged_rows(id) ON DELETE SET NULL DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this material belongs to. Half of the primary key.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

ingest.validate: set from the selected project, never from the CSV

columns.name: material_id
columns.meaning: The material's code as the user's own systems spell it. Joins to the BOM and to every inbound arc that supplies it.

engine.transform: str()

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: A human-readable name for the material. Display only.

engine.transform: str(name or material_id)

resolution.note: A label. Recorded for completeness: every engine-consumed field carries a resolution block, including the ones where the answer is trivial.

columns.name: cost
columns.meaning: What one unit of this material costs to buy. The master value; where it is unset the engine uses the cheapest inbound arc instead, which is usually what the user wants and is why leaving it blank is not an error.

engine.transform: float() when > 0
engine.missing_default: the cheapest inbound unit_price for this material, floored at 1.0

substitutions.value: the cheapest inbound arc's unit_price (grading.ts::cheapestInboundCost floors a <= 0 price to 1.0 first)
substitutions.visible_as: the effective-economics badge in /policies

resolution.note: hybrid is NULL because scsim has nowhere to put a spread: cost and unit_price are bare floats on Material and Product, with no distribution, no CV and no sampling path anywhere in the engine. Recording `hybrid: null` here is a statement about the ENGINE, not about the world — prices obviously vary. Giving them a spread is an engine change on the scsim track; see the RFC in PLAN.md §14. Do not invent one in this contract: a contract that describes a capability the engine does not have is how a fallback ends up in code with no contract entry, which is what I6 forbids in the other direction. estimable_from is empty for a second reason: the value already has a derivation — the cheapest inbound arc — and that is a substitution the user can see and trace, not an estimate.

engine_requirement.reason: Inventory valuation and holding cost — the terminal default of 1.0 makes every cost KPI meaningless.
engine_requirement.fallback: cheapest inbound unit_price across the material's suppliers

columns.name: holding_cost_pct
columns.unit: fraction of unit value per year
columns.meaning: The annual cost of holding one unit in stock, as a fraction of its value. 0.2 means holding a unit for a year costs a fifth of what the unit is worth.

engine.transform: falls back to the inventory policy bundle's holding_cost_pct when NULL
engine.missing_default: the project's inventory policy bundle value (0.2 in the shipped default)

substitutions.visible_as: the policy grid's provenance dot

resolution.note: A financial policy parameter, not an observation: it is what the business decides holding stock costs it. Falls back to the project's inventory bundle, which is a policy default and is visible as one.

columns.name: moq
columns.meaning: Minimum order quantity: the smallest amount this material can be ordered in. A commercial fact the supplier states, not something to be inferred from order history.

engine.transform: float(moq) when truthy, else 0.0 — applied per (supplier, material) link

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. A minimum order quantity is a term the supplier states. Inferring it from observed order sizes learns the ordering policy, not the constraint — and then the simulation optimises against its own past behaviour.

columns.name: initial_on_hand
columns.meaning: How much of this material is in stock when the simulation starts.

engine.transform: float() when not None; None is passed through as None, not as zero

resolution.note: Opening stock is a measurement — someone counted it — so it is the one master economic field where an observations tier could legitimately supply it. Nothing does today.

columns.name: lead_time_dist
columns.meaning: The SHAPE of this material's delivery lead time — deterministic, or a named distribution around the arc's lead time. `deterministic` means the lead time is exactly what the arc says, every time.

engine.transform: LeadTimeDist(value) when set, else LeadTimeDist.DETERMINISTIC

ingest.validate: one of the LeadTimeDist enum values; `empirical` is reserved for the data-import path (M7) and is not selectable yet

resolution.note: The SPREAD half of lead_time's hybrid; the centre is inbound_logistics.lead_time. LeadTimeDist.EMPIRICAL exists in the enum and is RESERVED for the data-import path (M7) — it is the value an estimator would write, which is why it is not offered in the UI today. `deterministic` is the default and means the lead time is exactly what the arc says.

columns.name: lead_time_cv
columns.meaning: How much the lead time varies, as a coefficient of variation. Read only when `lead_time_dist` is not deterministic: the engine skips sampling entirely when the distribution is deterministic or the CV is zero.

engine.transform: float() when truthy, else 0.0

resolution.note: The magnitude of lead_time's spread. Read only when lead_time_dist is not deterministic: core/engine.py tests both, so a CV on a deterministic link is silently inert. Zero and NULL are the same thing here.

columns.meaning: When the row last changed. Server-set.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was inserted. Server-set.

columns.name: source_system
columns.meaning: Which external system this row came from, when it was synced rather than uploaded. NULL for a hand-uploaded or hand-edited row.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine, and correctly so: it is provenance, not a parameter. Read by the ERP connector (blueprint G18), which is the only writer. Kept, not a deletion candidate.

columns.name: source_external_id
columns.meaning: This row's identifier in the external system, so a re-sync can match it.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine; ERP-connector provenance, as source_system.

columns.name: source_synced_at
columns.meaning: When the external system last confirmed this row.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine; ERP-connector provenance, as source_system.

On a table nothing writes they will never fire, which is the point: the rule is about every tier-2 table, not about the ones that happen to be busy.

multi_tier_supply_chain.note:
DESCRIBED IN PHASE 3 / WP 3.2, AND THE DESCRIPTION IS MOSTLY A LIST OF ABSENCES. The deferral that pointed here called these "the other inbound datasets, each with its own bespoke upload path". `tier2_suppliers` and `tier3_suppliers` are that; this table is not. NO APPLICATION PATH PUTS A ROW IN IT: `UploadWizard` offers no template, no screen and no edge function writes it, and no CSV names a column of it — which is why every `ingest.csv_header` above is null. THE DATABASE HAS A WRITE PATH ANYWAY, and the third correction WP 6.2 made is this one. `bulk_insert_multi_tier_supply_chain` exists, it is already on `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts`'s list of tier-2 writers, and it works — `rehearsal/240` §6c calls it and reads the row back. What is true is that NOTHING CALLS IT: no file in `src/` or `supabase/functions/` names it, which is why the reader below is answered with an empty array on every real project. But an RPC with no caller is not an absent write path. This application runs as `anon` against permissive grants (D28), so anyone holding a PostgREST client is one call away from writing this table — the same sentence WP 4.1 wrote about the three legacy `ingest-*` functions before `ingest_legacy_upsert_lane` turned their target list into a whitelist in a migration. The claim is APPLICATION-level; the grant surface is WP 7.1's. AND "NO READER AND NO WRITER" WAS FALSE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, WHICH THIS FILE HAD ALREADY RECORDED AND ITS OWN PROSE DENIED. The `surfaces` block above lists THREE confirmed entries, and WP 6.2 verified all of them against a real database: · `get_project_datasets` SELECTs this table and returns its rows, and
  `projectLanes.ts` calls it from `/policies` and `/simulation-lab` — so it HAS a
  live reader, feeding two pages.
· `delete_project_dataset` has a `multi_tier` branch AND deletes from this table
  in its `'all'` branch, which is what the "Delete ALL data" button on the project
  manager invokes — so it has a live path that EMPTIES it.
Two statements of one fact, in ONE FILE, disagreeing, with nothing comparing them: §4 D101's shape one scope tighter, and the generated page renders the PROSE half, so the contradiction was published to users. `supabase/rehearsal/240` §6 inserts a row, reads it back through the reader and watches the button's RPC remove it. `contract:check` R15 now refuses a note that denies a surface the same file confirms. What is true, stated once: nothing WRITES it, two pages READ it, and one button CLEARS it. Every occurrence is in migrations — created 2025-08-20, carried through RLS rewrites since, most recently by `20260915000004`'s organization dual read, which rewrote policies governing access to a table nobody can reach. EVERY `ingest.csv_header` ABOVE IS NULL FOR THAT REASON: there is no CSV to name a column of. It is described here rather than deferred again because a deferral is a promise that someone will look, and five packages of looking have now established what there is to see. DROPPING IT WAS NOT WP 3.2'S CALL — a table is not removed by the package that happened to notice. Its gap check added the count to §15 so that the package which does decide is deciding against a number, AND THE NUMBER IS ZERO: run `35143830532`, 2026-09-16, reports 0 rows across 0 projects, and run `35399391429`, 2026-09-19, agrees. WP 6.2 IS THE DECIDING PACKAGE AND ITS DECISION IS TO KEEP THE TABLE. The number says the benefit of dropping it is removing an empty relation. The cost, measured: rewriting `delete_project_dataset` — a live RPC behind a user-facing button — rewriting both dataset-snapshot builders, bumping `hash_network`'s `schema_version` 3 -> 4, which invalidates every stored network digest, deleting a published manual page and its registry entry, and updating four test files and a rehearsal — AND, found by the gate above, rewriting `get_project_datasets`, which two pages call on every load. That is a large and IRREVERSIBLE production change whose only gain is tidiness, taken against a row count measured days earlier. The table contributes an empty array to every project's `hash_network` today and costs nothing measurable. THE DECISION RESTS ON THE CORRECTED FACTS AND NOT THE ROW'S. §4 D58 argued from "no reader and no writer", and had the drop been taken on that premise it would have broken a reader two pages use. The number was right and the sentence beside it was not, which is the whole reason a decision waits for a measurement. What WAS wrong is the published claim, and that is corrected above rather than left standing: a page telling users nothing touches this table, while a button does, is the same defect as D103.

This is one of the few tables where `audited: true` is literally true today — WP 2.3 is what makes the claim general. Read is open to any member of the org via the self-bridge policy below, which WP 2.1 rewrote: it matched the caller's TEXT org against `name` or `slug`, so renaming an organization revoked its own members' read on the row that had just been renamed. It now bridges on `id` first.

columns.meaning: The organization's identity. Not displayable, and that is the property that makes it safe as a join key (§2.1 `uuid-identity`).

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: The organization's display name, as an administrator typed it. EDITABLE and NOT UNIQUE — two organizations may legitimately share one. It is a label for humans and it is never an identity.
columns.note: D13's join key. `admin_update_organization` updates this column and nothing else: no trigger, no cascade, and no second UPDATE reaching `approved_users.organization` or `projects.organization`. So a rename leaves those two text copies holding the OLD string, and the next user approved into the organization carries the NEW one — at which point a text comparison between them can never match again. WP 2.1 routes every such comparison through `org_is_current_user_org(uuid, text)`.

columns.name: slug
columns.meaning: A URL-safe form of the name, `lower(regexp_replace(name, '[^a-zA-Z0-9]+', '-', 'g'))` at the moment the row was seeded. UNIQUE, and deliberately NOT recomputed on rename — so after a rename it is a record of what the organization used to be called, which is what makes it usable to match rows written before it.

columns.name: owner_user_id
columns.meaning: The approved user who owns the tenant. Advisory today — nothing in RLS or any RPC reads it; ownership is expressed through `organization_members.org_role = 'owner'`. Two places holding the same fact is an I1 violation waiting to diverge; WP 2.2 owns the resolution.

A copy goes stale when the dataset moves; a decision does not, and marking it stale would tell the engine to distrust the one number somebody actually chose. Written by `bulk_upsert_policy_overrides`, which reads the hash from the project ITSELF rather than taking one from the caller — a caller that can supply provenance can supply the wrong provenance. ON CONFLICT it is overwritten, so typing over a seeded override clears it. Freshness is COMPUTED from it by `freshness_of` and never written back (§4 D70). **THE ENGINE READS OVERRIDES, NOT THE GRID**, so a stale value here is a simulation-correctness problem rather than a display one.

products.grain: One finished product in one project: the economics and the demand shape the simulation reads for it. Where this row is silent the engine derives price and demand from the outbound arcs.

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all thirteen sidecars change together. SEPARATELY — AND THIS REPLACES WHAT WP 1.2 WROTE HERE, WHICH WAS WRONG: this sidecar used to assert `rls_enabled: false` and say "no migration ever runs ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on them". One does. `20260614000001_item_master.sql:57-66` enables RLS and creates two policies (`%s_auth_all`, `%s_anon_read`) on each of the three masters — but through `EXECUTE format(...)` inside a `FOREACH` over an array of table names, which a static replay of the migrations cannot evaluate. The introspector recorded the absence as `enabled: false`, WP 1.2 read that as fact, and the contract was one generated page away from telling a user their item masters were unprotected. WP 1.4 fixed the mechanism, not the guess: the introspector now records dynamic DDL (`dynamic_ddl`) and marks the tables it touches `rls.determinate: false`, the validator refuses to let a sidecar assert an RLS state the migrations do not settle, and the generated page says the state is indeterminate and names the migration. The ONLY way to know is to read the live database — PLAN.md §15, still unrun. WP 2.4's security review owns it.

columns.name: production_capacity
columns.meaning: How much of this product the plant can make per week. The canonical G4 example: when it is unset the engine invents a capacity generous enough that capacity never binds, so an unset value silently turns off the constraint the user thinks they are simulating.

engine.transform: float() when > 0
engine.missing_default: max(2 x demand, 1000) — a value chosen so the constraint never binds

substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. This is the canonical G4 field: unset, the engine invents max(2 x demand, 1000), which is chosen so the constraint never binds. Estimating it from output would do the same thing with more ceremony — output is bounded by demand, so the fitted capacity can never explain a shortage.

engine_requirement.reason: With no capacity source the engine defaults to max(2·demand, 1000), so plant capacity never binds.

project_erp_links.grain: One authorized link between one project and one company in one external system: project ownership proved on this side, company membership proved on that side by the linking user's own OAuth consent. One link is one credential and one project — never shared, so revoking one project's link cannot be bypassed by a sibling.

governance.note: One FOR ALL policy — `has_project_access(project_id)` — so reading and writing a link are the same permission: whoever can administer the project can connect it to a source and disconnect it. That is deliberate and it is also the loosest thing on this page, because `min_project_role: owner` is the intent and nothing enforces a project role yet (WP 2.2 landed the resolver; no policy here calls it). `audited: false` is the one that should be uncomfortable: creating a link grants an external system standing access to a project's data and revoking one takes it away, and neither writes an audit row. It is not a tier transition, so G4 does not formally cover it; it is a governance event by any reading of §5, and it is recorded here as a named gap rather than left to be noticed. The table's own honesty is elsewhere and it is real: `status`, `status_detail`, `last_verified_at` and `revoked_at` mean a revoked link says when and why. NO `rls_enabled` FIELD, and its absence is the point. The connector migration enables RLS on this table in a plain statement and creates its policy in another — but the same file also builds the staging policies inside a `DO $$ EXECUTE format(...) $$` loop whose SQL mentions this table, so the introspector marks its RLS indeterminate: "the migrations do not say", which is a different claim from "off" and may not be rendered as one. Only the live database can answer (§15), and a sidecar may not assert what the schema does not settle.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. The link's identity for every run that used it.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The SuReSuite project this link feeds. One side of the two-sided grant.

columns.name: external_system
columns.meaning: Which external system — `orbit-mrp` is the only value any code writes. Free text, not CHECK-constrained, and that is the one place this table still assumes a single vendor: `ingest_runs.source_kind` is the closed vocabulary WP 3.1 added, and it is the one a reader should trust.
columns.note: A second connector would add a value here AND a `source_kind`, and the two would have to agree. Whoever adds it: make this column a CHECK, or derive it. Two vocabularies for one fact is what I1 exists to prevent, and this is the half WP 3.1 did not close.

columns.name: external_company_id
columns.meaning: The company/tenant identifier IN THE EXTERNAL SYSTEM. Part of the natural key with the project and the system: one project may link one company of one system exactly once.

columns.name: external_company_name
columns.meaning: The company's display name, cached for the picker and refreshed on each sync. A LABEL and never a key (G1) — the id above is what the grant is about.

columns.name: linked_by_user_id
columns.meaning: The person whose own OAuth consent proved membership of that company, in `auth.users`. NOT NULL because the link IS that proof: there is no way to create one from a hand-typed company id, and an unattributed link would be a credential with no owner.

columns.name: external_oauth_token_ref
columns.meaning: The NAME of a secret in Supabase Vault, never a token. `get_erp_oauth_token(p_ref)` resolves it and is granted to `service_role` only, so a browser session cannot read the credential even though it can read this row.
columns.note: The pointer is readable by any project member and the value is not. That is the design: a per-link, per-user delegated token, so revoking one project's link cannot be bypassed by a sibling project.

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: active, needs_attention or revoked. A sync re-verifies both sides before touching data and revokes the link on failure rather than continuing on the old assumption.
columns.note: Not an engine input. It is the field the sync path reads first, and `revoked` is terminal: the connector never resurrects a link, a person re-links.

columns.name: status_detail
columns.meaning: Why the status is what it is, in words a user can act on — "Access revoked in orbit-mrp — reconnect". The reason a revoked link is not a mystery.

columns.name: last_verified_at
columns.meaning: When both sides were last proved live. The age of the claim that this link still works.

columns.name: auto_apply_threshold_pct
columns.meaning: The percentage of changed rows below which a sync may promote itself without a human. 0 — the default — means every sync waits for approval.
columns.note: A number with teeth: above it, staged rows reach tier 2 with no person in the loop, and the resulting audit row names no actor (D36). It is bounded 0..100 by CHECK, and the connector additionally refuses to auto-apply any run with `fields_failed > 0`.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the link was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: revoked_at
columns.meaning: When the link was revoked, or NULL. With `status_detail`, the revocation is a record rather than a disappearance.

columns.name: sync_schedule_cron
columns.meaning: A cron expression for scheduled syncs, or NULL for manual-only. Read by the pg_cron sweep and by any external scheduler driving the same RPC.

columns.name: sync_enabled
columns.meaning: Whether the schedule is live. Two fields rather than one because a paused schedule must not lose its expression — turning sync off and on again should not require retyping the cron.
columns.note: Not an engine input. `due_erp_sync_links()` reads it with `status = 'active'` and a non-null cron; its own comment records that it is a placeholder that does not evaluate the expression, so today the sweep offers every enabled link and the Edge Function decides.

project_erp_links.note: NOT RENAMED BY WP 3.1, AND THAT IS A DECISION. The four tables around it became `ingest_*` because they hold rows from ANY source; this one holds the credential and the consent for ONE source, and calling it `ingest_links` would promise a generality it does not have — a CSV upload has nothing to link. When a second connector arrives, the question to ask is whether it shares this shape (a per-user delegated token proving membership of an external tenant) or needs its own; `ingest_runs.source_kind` already carries the distinction that matters to everything downstream. ITS SIDECAR IS HERE BECAUSE WP 3.1 IS WHERE IT WAS DUE. The table was deferred under this package in `coverage.yaml` since WP 1.4, and a deferral is a commitment: carrying it forward to the next open package would have been the same move that produced D41 — an owner who has gone home, indistinguishable from an owner.

The table has a SELECT policy and NO insert/update/delete policy, so RLS denies writes by default and the SECURITY DEFINER RPCs are the only way in. That is not an oversight to be tidied up later: D28 says every policy here is PERMISSIVE and permissive policies OR, so a "deny writes" policy added beside anything else would deny nothing. The ABSENCE of a policy is the enforcement. `audited: false` — a membership change writes no audit row; WP 2.3 is where that becomes true, and this table is one of the reasons it matters.

projects.grain: One modelling project: a named supply chain, owned by one modeller, belonging to one organization. It is the scope every other project-scoped table hangs off `project_id`, and it is the row almost every RLS policy in the schema reaches through to decide whether the caller may see anything at all.

governance.note: Tier G rather than a data tier: `projects` holds no measured quantity. It is the SCOPE, and its access rules are the ones every other table inherits by joining to it — which is why WP 2.1 had to redefine 58 policies on 24 other tables to change one comparison. Read is org-wide (any member of the owning organization sees every project in it); write is restricted to the project's own modeller or a global `admin`. There is no project-level role between those two — a member cannot be given read on one project and not another, which is `subtractive-delegation` (§2.1 G3) having nowhere to attach. WP 2.2's `project_members` is where `min_project_role: editor` above stops being a forward declaration. `audited: false`: project creation and deletion write no audit row (WP 2.3).

risk_data.note: The second of WP 1.4's three orphans (D4), and the one that turned out not to be an orphan at all. Two network pages read it and no migration created it — but the table EXISTS in the production database, untracked, with the spreadsheet-header columns `COUNTRY` and `"RISK CLASS"`. CI proved it: the first version of the migration was a plain `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, which no-opped, and the next statement failed on a column that was not there. Same class as `approved_users`: created outside migration tracking, invisible to a static replay, which can only tell you no migration creates a table and not whether one exists. `20260915000003_risk_data.sql` now both builds it on a fresh database and ADOPTS the one already there — renaming the quoted columns, adding the provenance columns, and marking the pre-contract rows `source: 'unrecorded (loaded before the reference-tier contract)'` rather than inventing a publisher for them. The new CHECKs land `NOT VALID` on the adopted table: enforced for every future write, not retroactively asserted about rows nobody has looked at.

WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all thirteen sidecars change together. SEPARATELY — AND THIS REPLACES WHAT WP 1.2 WROTE HERE, WHICH WAS WRONG: this sidecar used to assert `rls_enabled: false` and say "no migration ever runs ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on them". One does. `20260614000001_item_master.sql:57-66` enables RLS and creates two policies (`%s_auth_all`, `%s_anon_read`) on each of the three masters — but through `EXECUTE format(...)` inside a `FOREACH` over an array of table names, which a static replay of the migrations cannot evaluate. The introspector recorded the absence as `enabled: false`, WP 1.2 read that as fact, and the contract was one generated page away from telling a user their item masters were unprotected. WP 1.4 fixed the mechanism, not the guess: the introspector now records dynamic DDL (`dynamic_ddl`) and marks the tables it touches `rls.determinate: false`, the validator refuses to let a sidecar assert an RLS state the migrations do not settle, and the generated page says the state is indeterminate and names the migration. The ONLY way to know is to read the live database — PLAN.md §15, still unrun. WP 2.4's security review owns it.

governance.note: Two policies, both routed through the project's organization — `org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization)` for SELECT and the same predicate plus modeler-or-admin for writes. Writing this sidecar turned that gate red in the same session, and `20260916000016` is the gate being obeyed rather than a decision taken. It matters here more than most: `ingest_apply_run` promotes a CSV into this table, and a promotion into an unaudited table is the `audit-actor` hole this package exists to close.
