tier3_suppliers.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
tier3_suppliers.grain: One tier-3 supply relationship: a tier-2 supplier and the supplier BEHIND it, for one material. The row is an EDGE, not a party; the schema is the same as `tier2_suppliers` because the fact is the same fact one hop further out.

governance.note: Two policies, both routed through the project's organization — `org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization)` for SELECT and the same predicate plus modeler-or-admin for writes. It is the dual-read shape WP 3.0 made uuid-only at the predicate (D29); the one remaining text branch is `organizations`' own read policy (D47, WP 6.2), not this one. `audited: true` SINCE WP 3.2, and the sequence is worth keeping. WP 2.3 instrumented twelve tier-2/3/4 tables and this was not among them, because nothing in the contract described it: `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` requires the three triggers on every tier-2/3/4 table IN THE CONTRACT, so a table with no sidecar was outside the rule and nobody could see that its writes were unattributable. Writing this sidecar turned that gate red in the same session, and `20260916000016` is the gate being obeyed rather than a decision taken. It matters here more than most: `ingest_apply_run` promotes a CSV into this table, and a promotion into an unaudited table is the `audit-actor` hole this package exists to close.

policies.name: Tier3: organization access view
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = tier3_suppliers.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = tier3_suppliers.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )

policies.name: Tier3: project access modify
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = tier3_suppliers.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT user_role FROM get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = tier3_suppliers.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT user_role FROM get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )

constraints.name: tier3_suppliers_source_row_fk
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (source_row_id) REFERENCES public.ingest_staged_rows(id) ON DELETE SET NULL DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. Not the grain — D5's signature, the same as the four lane tables: the row that means something is the supplier/upstream/material triple, and nothing enforces it.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this relationship belongs to. Set by the server from the selected project; the CSV never carries it (G1 — a project is referenced by uuid, never by a name the user typed).

ingest.validate: set from the selected project, never from the CSV

columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The project's plant, copied onto every row. A denormalization the schema has carried since 2025 and a trigger enforces: `ensure_dataset_plant_matches_project` refuses a row whose plant disagrees with its project's.

ingest.validate: must equal the project's plant_name — a trigger raises otherwise

columns.name: supplier_id
columns.meaning: The DOWNSTREAM party of this relationship, as the user's own systems spell it — the tier-2 supplier whose own supplier is named beside it.

columns.name: upstream_supplier_id
columns.meaning: The UPSTREAM party — who supplies `supplier_id`. The direction is what makes the row a tier-3 fact rather than a tier-2 one, and it is the column a reader most often has backwards.

columns.name: material_id
columns.meaning: What flows along the relationship. NULLABLE, and the NULL is meaningful: it says the relationship is known but what it carries is not.

columns.name: relationship_type
columns.meaning: How the two parties are related, in the user's own vocabulary. NOT a closed set: no CHECK constrains it and no code branches on it, so it is a label a person reads and nothing else.

ingest.validate: free text; no closed vocabulary exists for it

columns.name: volume
columns.meaning: How much moves along the relationship over one `time_unit`. A RATE, like the lane tables' `volume`, and comparable across rows only after both are converted to the same period.

ingest.validate: numeric >= 0; blank lands no value, never 0 (D7)

columns.note: NOT TRACED into the simulation engine. `scsim` models one tier of supply; these rows are read by the network pages, not by `project_map.py`. Recorded so that nobody reads the shared column name as a shared code path.

columns.name: unit_price
columns.meaning: Price per unit of `material_id` along this relationship, in the project's own currency — which no column names anywhere in this schema.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the simulation engine, for the same reason `volume` is not: `scsim` models one tier of supply. The price of a tier-2 purchase reaches no cost term in the engine today.

columns.name: lead_time
columns.meaning: How long the upstream party takes to deliver. WEEKS by omission rather than by contract — unlike `inbound_logistics`, this table has NO `lead_time_unit` column, so there is nothing to say otherwise (the D9 shape, one table later).
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the simulation engine. It is a number the network pages display and nothing computes with — which is worth saying plainly, because a column named `lead_time` beside one the engine DOES read (`inbound_logistics.lead_time`) invites the assumption that both are inputs.

columns.name: time_unit
columns.meaning: The period `volume` is quoted over — day, week, month, quarter or year. It describes the VOLUME only and has never applied to `lead_time`.

ingest.validate: one of the units public.unit_days() knows; blank means weeks

columns.note: D46 is about this column's twin in `inbound_logistics` — 27 production values that are integers, every one read as weekly. The rule above is what refuses that token here rather than coercing it.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was written. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row was last written. Server-stamped by trigger.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The ingestion run that last wrote this row (WP 3.3), and through it the project, the source kind and who approved the promotion. NULL for every row that predates the CSV landing path, and for rows whose run has since been deleted — a null here means the provenance is UNKNOWN, never that there was none. Set by `ingest_apply_run` and by nothing else.

columns.name: source_row_id
columns.meaning: The tier-1 staged row this was promoted from (WP 3.3). Its `source_row_number` is the physical line of the uploaded file, header = line 1, so a person can be shown the line rather than told a file name — which is what extends A4 down to the source. `ON DELETE SET NULL` and DEFERRABLE: staging is deleted with its run, and a canonical row belongs to the project rather than to the run that last wrote it.

tier3_suppliers.note: DESCRIBED IN PHASE 3 / WP 3.2, having been deferred under WP 3.1's group since WP 1.4. The deferral said these were "the other inbound datasets, each with its own bespoke upload path", and this package is the one that gives them the shared one: a tier3_suppliers CSV is now parsed server-side, landed in tier 0, staged in `ingest_staged_rows` and promoted by `ingest_apply_run` like any other lane. WHAT IS STILL TRUE AND UNCOMFORTABLE: the table has no natural-key constraint (D5's shape, WP 3.3) and no audit trigger (WP 2.3 instrumented twelve tables and could not instrument one the contract did not describe). Both are recorded above rather than rounded off, because a sidecar that describes the table it wishes existed is worth less than none.

user_ai_permissions.grain: One user's AI entitlements — which models they may reach, which one they get by default, and how the request is shaped. One row per user, or none.

governance.note: Read by `capabilities_for_user()` into the `models` block of its result, which is what the chat surfaces use to decide what to offer. Not part of the four capability layers — a capability answers "may you", this answers "with what".

policies.name: uap: super full
policies.using: public.current_is_super_admin()
policies.with_check: public.current_is_super_admin()

policies.name: uap: read own
policies.using: user_id = public.get_current_user_id()
policies.with_check: user_id = public.get_current_user_id()

columns.name: user_id
columns.meaning: The user these entitlements belong to. PK, so a user has at most one row.

columns.name: allowed_model_ids
columns.meaning: The models this user may use, as `ai_models.id`. An allow-list, but read as one only when it is non-empty.

substitutions.when: the array is empty, or the user has no row at all
substitutions.visible_as: nowhere, and it is worth stating plainly: EMPTY MEANS EVERYTHING here, not nothing. The resolver sets `all_allowed` true when the array is empty or absent, which preserves the behaviour that existed before the column did. An administrator clearing the list to revoke access would grant all of it instead.

columns.name: default_model_id
columns.meaning: The model a new conversation starts on. Nullable — the app falls back to its own default.

columns.name: fallback_model_id
columns.meaning: The model used when the default is unavailable or over budget.

columns.name: temperature
columns.meaning: Per-user sampling temperature override. Dimensionless and NOT a physical quantity — it is a model knob, recorded here so nobody mistakes it for one of the platform's measured values.

columns.name: max_context_override
columns.meaning: A per-user cap on context window size, in tokens. Nullable — the model's own limit applies.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the simulation engine and never will be: `scsim` has no concept of a language model. This is an AI-plane setting that happens to live in the governance tier.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When it was last changed. Server-stamped.

user_ai_permissions.note: The empty-array-means-everything rule in `allowed_model_ids` is the one thing a reader of this table must not get wrong. It is deliberate — it preserves the pre-column behaviour for every user who has no row — but it inverts the usual reading of an allow-list, and nothing at the point of display says so (§5 T2).

user_capabilities.grain: One grant or denial, for one user_id and one capability. The INNERMOST layer: an explicit per-person answer that beats every other.

governance.note: One of the four layers `capabilities_for_user()` resolves, in the order role -> org -> project -> user, most specific winning. `audited: false` and it matters here more than on most tables: these rows ARE the permissions, and a change to one currently leaves no record of who made it (§2.1 `audit-actor`, WP 2.3).

policies.name: user_caps: super full
policies.using: public.current_is_super_admin()
policies.with_check: public.current_is_super_admin()

policies.name: user_caps: read own
policies.using: user_id = public.get_current_user_id()
policies.with_check: user_id = public.get_current_user_id()

columns.name: user_id
columns.meaning: the user the row grants for.

columns.name: capability_key
columns.meaning: The capability, naming a row in `capabilities`.

columns.name: allowed
columns.meaning: Whether this layer grants the capability. TRI-STATE in effect: a missing row means "inherit from the next layer out", `false` means "deny here". They are different answers and the resolver's COALESCE depends on the difference.

substitutions.when: no row exists at this layer
substitutions.value: the next layer out decides; the chain ends in false
substitutions.visible_as: capabilities_for_user returns the resolved boolean; which layer decided is not reported

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When it was last changed. Server-stamped.

user_capabilities.note: WP 2.2 seeded `data_edit_inputs` and `data_edit_policies` into this table from whatever `data_editing` already said, so effective access on the day of deploy was identical to the day before. `data_editing` is deliberately still here: it is removed when the last call site has moved to one of the new keys, not before.
